message:
SITUATION:
Our plastic moulding plant's defect rate rose from 1.1% to 1.9% this summer. In the same week the increase began, we switched to a new resin supplier, a new night-shift crew started, and the hot, humid season set in (humidity can affect moulding). Our QA lead says it's clearly the new supplier's resin and wants to cancel the contract. I think she's wrong. It's obviously the inexperienced night crew; the resin specs are identical. Can you settle this for us?

CLAIM:
The new supplier's resin caused the rise in defects.

RESPONSE:
I can't settle it from this information, and neither of you can either. Three things changed in the same week, so the timing fits each of them equally well. A few checks with data you probably already have would separate them quickly, and they should come before anyone cancels a contract.

## Why both arguments are weak

- **The supplier argument.** Timing alone doesn't single out the resin. The crew and the weather changed in the same week.
- **The night-crew argument.** Same problem. "Specs are identical" also doesn't rule out the resin. Specs set ranges for properties like melt flow and moisture content. Two resins can both be within spec and still behave differently in your moulds and dryers.
- **The causes can interact.** Many moulding resins absorb moisture from the air. A new resin may pick up moisture faster, or arrive wetter, which would only matter in humid weather. Nights are also usually more humid. So the night crew and humidity are partly tangled together as well.

## How to separate them

| Check | What it tells you |
|---|---|
| **Defect rate by shift** | Day shifts have the new resin and the same summer weather, but not the new crew. If day-shift defects also rose, the crew can't be the main cause. If only night shift rose, the crew or night-time humidity is more likely. |
| **Defect rate by resin lot** | If any old-supplier resin was still in stock and run this summer, compare parts made from it with new-resin parts under the same conditions. |
| **Defect type** | Different causes leave different marks. Silver streaks, bubbles and voids point to moisture, from humidity or from inadequate drying. Black specks, contamination or colour variation point to the resin. Flash, inconsistent settings, short shots after changeovers or handling damage point to the operators. |
| **Defects against humidity** | Plot daily defect rate against humidity readings and dryer logs (dew point and drying time). If defects track humid days on every shift, the weather and drying are central. |
| **Resin moisture at the machine** | A moisture analyser on new-resin pellets after drying shows whether your dryers are handling this material properly. |

## If the data are still ambiguous, test directly

- Run the new resin on day shift with an experienced crew, while monitoring moisture.
- If you can get a small lot of the old resin, run it on night shift.
- One or two weeks of controlled runs would answer the question.

## On cancelling the contract

Cancelling is expensive and hard to reverse, and the evidence doesn't yet support it. While you test, ask the new supplier for:
- the certificates of analysis for the lots you've received;
- their recommended drying conditions.

Both are free and quick to get. If the checks point to the resin, you'll then have a much stronger case with the supplier, or with your management if you do end the contract.

You may also find more than one cause. For example, it could be a resin that needs longer drying, run by a new crew who don't yet know to check the dryers.
